title: Lighthouse Letters
subtitle: Perspective and Theme in Two Texts
summary: A museum has received a keeper's letter, his daughter's diary and a newspaper report about the same 1938 storm. Listen, read, compare two narrators' perspectives, retell the night, and write about a shared theme.

briefing.scene: The Cape Harrow Maritime Museum has received a box from the Ames family. Inside are a newspaper story, a keeper's letter and his daughter's diary, all about one stormy night in 1938. As the Archive Reader, you read each item closely before the exhibit opens.
briefing.goal: Explain how each narrator's perspective shapes what the reader learns, then write the wall text that names a theme the texts share.

gazette.title: Museum Audio Guide: The Gazette Report

turns.speaker: Ms. Okafor
turns.text: Welcome to the Cape Harrow Maritime Museum. This recording shares the news story printed in the Harrow Gazette on November 16, 1938. Our volunteer, Mr. Dunn, will read it.

turns.speaker: Mr. Dunn
turns.text: Keeper Saves Twenty-three Sailors. On the night of November 14, a winter storm drove the freighter Marguerite toward the rocks near Cape Harrow. Keeper Walter Ames climbed the lighthouse stairs at nine o'clock and kept the lamp burning until dawn, even after the wind broke a window in the lantern room. The crew of twenty-three steered by his beam and anchored safely in Dunmore Bay at six in the morning. Mr. Ames told this newspaper only, 'I did what the job requires.'

turns.speaker: Ms. Okafor
turns.text: The Gazette called the keeper calm and brave. But the museum also has his own letter, and a diary written by his daughter, Nell, who was twelve. As you read them, ask yourself whether each writer sees the night in the same way.

letter.title: Letter from Walter Ames to his brother, November 17, 1938
text: You have probably read in the Gazette that I am a hero. Please do not believe all of it. The paper makes the night sound like an adventure, but it was only a long night of work. The storm was bad, I will admit, but a keeper's job is simple: when the sky goes dark, the lamp must be lit.

Around nine o'clock the wind began to howl, and by midnight a window in the lantern room had shattered. I stuffed my coat into the frame. When the clockwork stuck, I turned the lens by hand, one slow circle after another. My fingers ached, but there was nothing unusual in that. The Marguerite was out there somewhere, and her crew needed one steady light.

At dawn the freighter slid into Dunmore Bay, and I climbed down the stairs. Nell was awake at the kitchen table, though I had told her to sleep. I only said good morning. Some mornings, words are not needed.

diary.title: Diary of Nell Ames, age 12, November 15, 1938
text: I was not supposed to be awake, but nobody could sleep in that wind. At midnight I heard glass break above us, so I crept up the stairs and stopped at the last step. Through the doorway of the lantern room I saw Papa. His coat was stuffed into the broken window, and he was turning the great lens by hand. His face looked calm, but his hands told the truth: they were shaking.

I wanted to help, but my legs would not move. So I sat on the cold stairs and counted each time the beam swept past the window. I counted one hundred and twelve before I lost track. Before sunrise I ran down to the kitchen so he would not know I had seen him. When he came in, he said only 'good morning,' and I poured his tea.
Maybe being brave does not mean being unafraid. Maybe it means turning the lens anyway.

logbook.title: The Keeper's Logbook

table.caption: Cape Harrow Light logbook, November 14-15, 1938
rows: Heavy rain. Freighter sighted off the point.
Lantern window broken. Clockwork stuck. Turning lens by hand.
Lens still turning. Freighter holding offshore.

logbook.summary: The keeper's logbook for November 14-15, 1938 records winds rising from 35 to 61 mph, a broken lantern window, a stuck clock, and the keeper turning the lens by hand until the freighter anchored safely at dawn.

donor-note.title: Note from the donor, Ben Carver, grandson of Walter Ames
text: My grandfather never spoke about the night of the Marguerite. When I asked him once, he said, 'It was a long night, and the lamp needed tending.' My mother, Nell, kept her diary in a shoebox for fifty years.
She told me she never let him know she had seen him in the lantern room. 'He would have been embarrassed,' she said. 'And I was prouder of him than ever.'
donor-note.summary: The donor says his grandfather never talked about the night of the Marguerite, and that his mother secretly watched him in the lantern room and was prouder of him than ever.

phases.title: Museum Audio Guide: The Gazette Report
phases.instructions: Listen to the audio guide. It reads a 1938 newspaper story about the storm. Listen twice if you need to. Then answer the questions without looking for a script.

tasks.q: According to the Gazette report, what did Keeper Ames do during the storm?

options.text: He rowed out to the Marguerite and carried the crew to shore.
He kept the lamp burning until dawn so the crew could steer.
He left the lighthouse to ask the town for help.
He broke a window in the lantern room to let more light out.

tasks.explain: The report says Ames 'kept the lamp burning until dawn' and that the crew 'steered by his beam.' The wind, not Ames, broke the window.

tasks.q: What can you infer about how Mr. Ames talks about his own actions?

options.text: He wants every sailor in the harbor to know his name.
He cannot remember what happened that night.
The crew of twenty-three anchored safely in Dunmore Bay.
He prefers to play down what he did.

tasks.explain: When the newspaper praised him, Ames said only, 'I did what the job requires.' A short, modest answer suggests he plays down his actions. The crew's safe landing is true, but it does not answer the question.

tasks.q: Choose the statements that tell what Keeper Ames actually DID during the storm.

pool.text: climbed the lighthouse stairs at nine o'clock
kept the lamp burning until dawn
The crew of twenty-three steered by his beam
The Gazette called the keeper calm and brave.
Our volunteer, Mr. Dunn, will read it.
I did what the job requires.

phases.title: Two Voices from One Night
phases.instructions: Read Walter's letter and Nell's diary. Think about who is telling each text and what that narrator notices, includes or leaves out.

tasks.q: In the letter, how does Walter see his own actions that night?

options.text: He sees them as ordinary work that a keeper must do.
He is proud that the Gazette called him a great hero.
He thinks no keeper should ever be praised for the job.
He is upset that Nell stayed awake in the kitchen.

tasks.explain: Walter writes, 'Please do not believe all of it' and 'there was nothing unusual in that.' He treats the night as duty, not heroism. He mentions Nell at the kitchen table without any anger.

tasks.q: What does Nell notice in the lantern room that Walter's letter never mentions?

options.text: He cried when the window shattered above him.
The wind broke a window in the lantern room.
His hands were shaking while he turned the lens.

tasks.explain: Nell writes that 'his hands told the truth: they were shaking.' Walter's letter does mention the broken window, so that detail is not new.

tasks.q: Why does Nell run down to the kitchen before her father comes down?

options.text: She wants him to see that she was watching over him.
She does not want him to know she saw his hands shaking.
She is angry that he did not ask her to help.
Her father told her to sleep, so she is afraid of being punished.

tasks.explain: Nell says she ran down 'so he would not know I had seen him.' Together with her remark about his hands, this suggests she protects his privacy. Walter's order to sleep appears only in his letter.

tasks.q: What does a reader learn by reading BOTH the letter and the diary?

options.text: Walter stayed calm all night, just as his letter says.
Lighthouse keepers are never afraid of any storm.
Nell wrote her diary to prove her father's letter was false.
The letter shows his duty; the diary shows the fear he hid.

tasks.explain: Walter's letter describes duty and downplays danger. Nell's diary adds what he kept private. Each narrator's perspective is partial, so the two texts together give a fuller picture.

tasks.q: Which theme do the letter and the diary share?

options.text: Doing duty quietly can be a form of courage.
A lighthouse works only when its clockwork works.
Real courage means feeling no fear at all.
A keeper's job is to keep the lamp lit all night.

tasks.explain: Walter keeps the lamp lit as plain duty. Nell concludes that 'being brave does not mean being unafraid.' Together they show courage as quiet duty. The last option states the setting of the duty but leaves out the idea of courage.

tasks.q: What does Nell mean when she writes that her father's 'hands told the truth'?

options.text: Walter wrote the truth about the storm in his letter.
His hands were too cold to hold the lens well.
His body showed a fear that his calm face hid.

tasks.explain: Nell says his face looked calm 'but' his hands were shaking. The word 'but' shows a contrast between what his face said and what his hands showed.

phases.title: Choose the Next Archive Item
phases.instructions: The museum can pull one more item from the archive before you plan the exhibit label. Choose one. Either choice leads to a complete mission.

decision.q: Which archive item do you request first?

options.text: The keeper's logbook from November 14-15, 1938
options.consequence: The logbook records the storm in numbers: wind of 61 miles per hour and a quarter mile of visibility at 12:15 a.m. The facts show the night was more dangerous than Walter's letter suggests.

board.label: Logbook
board.text: At 12:15 a.m. the wind reached 61 mph and visibility fell to one-quarter mile.

board.label: Logbook
board.text: Walter's log entry was short and factual: 'Turning lens by hand.'

options.text: A note from the donor, Nell's son
options.consequence: The note shows that Walter never spoke about the night and that Nell kept her secret for fifty years. It helps you explain why the two texts feel so different.

board.label: Donor note
board.text: Walter never spoke about the night; he said only, 'the lamp needed tending.'

board.label: Donor note
board.text: Nell kept her diary for fifty years and never told her father she had seen him.

phases.title: Audio Guide: Nell's Version
phases.instructions: Record a short audio-guide stop. Speak as Nell and keep her perspective.

task.title: Retell the Night as Nell
task.scenario: You are recording a 60-second stop for the museum audio guide. Visitors have just heard the Gazette report and want to know how it felt to be in the lighthouse that night.
task.prompt: Retell the storm night as Nell, using 'I.' Tell what you saw, what you did, and what you understood about your father. If you opened the logbook or the donor note, add one fact from your board.

text: Nell's diary: 'Through the doorway of the lantern room I saw Papa. His coat was stuffed into the broken window, and he was turning the great lens by hand. His face looked calm, but his hands told the truth: they were shaking.'
Nell's diary: 'Before sunrise I ran down to the kitchen so he would not know I had seen him. When he came in, he said only good morning, and I poured his tea.'
Walter's letter: 'My fingers ached, but there was nothing unusual in that.'

planner.label: Where I was
planner.hint: Say where you stood and why you were awake.

planner.label: What I saw
planner.hint: Describe your father in the lantern room.

planner.label: What I did
planner.hint: Tell what you did on the stairs and in the kitchen.

planner.label: What I understood
planner.hint: End with what you learned about being brave.

frames: Now I understand that being brave means ___.
guided.model: That night I was on the stairs because nobody could sleep in the wind. Through the doorway of the lantern room I saw Papa turning the lens by hand. His face looked calm, but his hands told the truth: they were shaking. Before sunrise I ran down to the kitchen so he would not know I had seen him. Now I understand that being brave means doing your duty even when you are afraid.

successCriteria: I tell the story in first person, as Nell.
I use at least two details from the diary.
I use time words such as 'before sunrise' or 'when' to keep the order clear.
I end with what Nell understands about courage.

listenFor: First-person narration that stays in Nell's voice
A concluding statement about courage, not only a list of events
teacher.followUp: What does Nell know that her father does not know?

phases.title: Wall Text: A Theme in Two Voices
phases.instructions: Write the paragraph for the wall beside the letter and the diary.

task.title: A Theme in Two Voices
task.scenario: The museum curator needs one paragraph for the wall beside the letter and the diary. It must explain a theme the two texts share to visitors who have not read them.
task.prompt: Write one paragraph that states a theme shared by Walter's letter and Nell's diary. Support it with one piece of evidence from each text, and explain how each narrator's perspective helps the reader see the theme.

frames: Both texts show the theme that ___.
In the letter, Walter says ___, which shows ___.
In the diary, Nell writes ___, which shows ___.
Together, the two perspectives help the reader understand that ___.
guided.model: Both texts show the theme that courage can be quiet duty. In the letter, Walter says, 'there was nothing unusual in that,' which shows he treats his work as ordinary. In the diary, Nell writes that 'his hands told the truth,' which shows he was afraid but kept going. Together, the two perspectives help the reader understand that being brave means doing what is needed even when you are afraid.

revisionPrompts.prompt: Did you include a quotation or close paraphrase from BOTH texts? Add the one you are missing.
Add a sentence that explains how Walter's perspective and Nell's perspective are different.
Add a connecting phrase such as 'In contrast' or 'Together' between your two pieces of evidence.

successCriteria: I state one theme in a complete sentence.
I use one detail from the letter and one from the diary.
I explain how the narrators' perspectives help show the theme.

lookFor: A theme (not just a topic such as 'storms')
Reasoning that names each narrator's perspective
commonIssues: Retelling the plot without naming a theme
Treating Walter's calm letter as the whole truth

teacherQuestions: Walter and Nell lived the same night. Which details did each narrator choose, and which did each leave out?
How did the extra item you chose (logbook or donor note) change what you could say about the theme?
Where in your paragraph did you separate what the text says from what you infer?
debrief.connections: Compare this to any pair of texts where two people describe the same event, such as a news report and a personal account. Ask students how a narrator's relationship to the event changes what is emphasized, and how a reader can use more than one source to find a theme.
